quote: water cascading into the circle below
context: The stream the poets have been following across the sand reaches the inner edge of the seventh circle and drops over a great cliff into the eighth.

note: Three famous Florentines of the generation before Dante's, all leaders of the Guelph party. They belong to a different band of sodomites from Brunetto's scholars in Canto 15: this one holds soldiers and statesmen.
Each Italian city had its own style of dress. Dante's long gown and hood mark him as a Florentine.

context: The canto sets the Florence of these three men, remembered as brave and courteous, against the money-mad city of 1300.

note: Virgil's respect is striking. He says that, but for the fire, it would be Dante's place to run to them. Dante condemns their sin and still honors what they did for their city.

quote: all three formed themselves into a wheel
note: The souls of this ring may never stand still (Canto 15). To talk with Dante, who has stopped, they turn in a circle on the spot, twisting their necks to keep their eyes on him.
The image is of athletes of the ancient kind, circling and watching for a hold. It gives these scorched men something of the dignity of champions.
Like most of the damned, they care above all about how they are remembered among the living.

Daughter of Bellincion Berti, a Florentine of the old stock whom Dante praises in Paradiso 15 and 16. She was a byword for beauty and modesty. A popular story had her refuse a kiss to the emperor Otto IV, saying that no man but her husband would ever kiss her.

context: Wisdom and sword: he was known both as a counselor and as a commander.
Dante's Italian says his voice should have been welcome in the world above, which is usually taken to mean his ignored advice against the war with Siena. Dante asked after him by name in Inferno 6.
He is the speaker, and the least grand of the three. Dante asked after him too in Inferno 6, and was told he lay among the blacker souls further down.

note: Early commentators say her temper was so bad that he left her and turned away from women altogether. He blames her for his sin.

quote: I would have thrown myself down among them
note: Dante wants to embrace them, as he could not embrace Brunetto. Nowhere else in Hell does he show such warmth toward a group of the damned.
Virgil, whose words a moment ago told Dante that these were men to be honored.
Dante's word is gall. He is leaving the bitterness of sin for the sweet fruit of salvation, which Virgil has promised lies at the end of the journey.
The way to salvation runs all the way down first, to the center of the earth where Satan is fixed, before it can turn upward.
The two great virtues of the knightly ideal: courage and worth on one side, generosity and good manners on the other. For Dante they sum up the old Florence that is gone.

Guglielmo Borsiere, a Florentine known as a witty and well-mannered man of the courts. Little else is recorded of him. Since he has only just arrived, he must have died shortly before 1300. Boccaccio made him the hero of a story in the Decameron.

Dante's Italian says "the new people and the sudden gains". The new people are families lately come in from the countryside, who grew rich fast in trade and banking. Dante blames them for the city's pride and its feuds, a theme he returns to in Paradiso 16.
He does not answer the three men directly. He lifts his head and shouts at Florence itself, far above him on the surface of the earth.
They admire his blunt answer and hint at its price. Speaking the truth this plainly will cost Dante dearly, in exile.
The stars are what the damned will never see again. Each of the poem's three parts ends on the word stars, and Inferno closes with Dante coming out to see them once more.
A measure of time from church: the moment it takes to say the word that ends a prayer.

The Montone. In Dante's day it was the first river on the north-eastern side of the Apennines, counting eastward from Monviso, to reach the Adriatic by its own course. All those before it ran into the Po.
Monviso, a peak in the western Alps where the river Po rises.
The name means quiet water. It is what the stream is called in the mountains, above its waterfall. Lower down, by Forlì, it is the Montone.
A monastery in the Apennines on the road from Florence to Forlì, near the Acquacheta falls. Dante probably knew the place from his years of exile.

quote: where a thousand streams could fit
note: A disputed line. The Italian says only "where there should be room for a thousand". Some take it as this translation does: one drop does the work of a thousand smaller falls. Others take it of the monastery, which had room for many more monks than it held.

quote: a cord wound around my waist
note: One of the poem's unsolved puzzles. The cord has never been mentioned before. It has been read as the cord of a Franciscan, since an old tradition says Dante was close to the order in his youth, as a sign of chastity or of self-confidence, and in other ways. No reading has won general agreement.

quote: the leopard with the spotted hide
context: The first of the three beasts of Canto 1. Nothing was said there about a plan to catch it with a cord.

quote: cast it down into the deep abyss
note: A signal, or a bait, for the creature that lives below. The eighth circle lies far down a sheer drop, and the poets need something to carry them.
Virgil often answers what Dante has only thought. As the voice of reason, he sees into Dante's mind.

A wise man keeps quiet about a true thing no one will believe, since it only makes him look a liar. Dante says this just as he is about to describe the monster of fraud, and swears that this incredible thing is true.

The first time the poem is named. Dante called it simply the Comedy: a work that begins in misery and ends in joy, written in the everyday language rather than in Latin. "Divine" was added by admirers later, and first appeared on the title page of an edition printed in 1555.

context: He comes up through the dark air like a swimmer rising through water. Dante holds back his name and his looks until the next canto.

note: A sailor who has gone down to free a stuck anchor and now kicks back up to the surface, arms reaching and legs drawn in.
